claims.text: Traditional fusion-welding repair of the target high-value component would pose a hot-cracking risk.
Increasing the SPS consolidation temperature improves particle diffusion, homogenization, pore closure, and densification of mechanically alloyed HEA powders.
Higher-temperature SPS produces a denser and more uniform multiphase HEA electrode microstructure than lower-temperature SPS.
Electrodes made by higher-temperature SPS produce more continuous and adherent ESD coatings.
Increasing the number of ESD layers causes superficial oxidation, roughness, and microfissuring.
Pulsed spark melting during ESD forms a chemically mixed, continuous HEA coating.
A lower-porosity, mechanically robust coating bond to the steel substrate mitigates the hot-cracking problems associated with fusion welding.
Higher-temperature SPS combined with six-layer ESD yields better densification than lower-temperature SPS combined with three-layer ESD.
Higher-temperature SPS combined with six-layer ESD yields greater elemental homogenization than lower-temperature SPS combined with three-layer ESD.
Higher-temperature SPS combined with six-layer ESD yields greater overall structural integrity than lower-temperature SPS combined with three-layer ESD.
The resulting coatings can perform effectively under aggressive operating conditions.
The SPS/ESD process provides a viable repair alternative that avoids the hot-cracking risks of traditional fusion welding.
The proposed feedstocks are mechanically alloyed CrFeNiMo, Co0.5CrFeNiMo, and Al0.5CrFeNiMo powders milled for 30 hours in N-heptane and sieved to 80 micrometers or less.
The proposed substrate is polished and degreased low-carbon C1018 steel.

The proposed SPS schedule uses 50 MPa pressure, a 50 degrees Celsius per minute heating rate, a 5-minute target-temperature dwell, and a 30 degrees Celsius per minute cooling rate in graphite tooling.
The proposed ESD process uses an argon flow of 5 liters per minute and an electrode angle of approximately 45 degrees.
For CrFeNiMo, the proposed ESD electrical settings include 30 microfarads, 100 volts, and 360 hertz.
Performance in corrosive, simulated geothermal, or other extremely aggressive media has not yet been validated.
Long-term performance under aggressive exposure and the trade-off between layer count, oxidation, and microcrack formation remain uncertain.
SEM/EDS, XRD, Archimedes density, Vickers hardness, and coating-mass measurements can test the predicted microstructural and mechanical differences between processing conditions.
